items.content_text:
A $25 MILLION INVESTMENT IN THE FUTURE OF CHATTANOOGA!
 Today, CARTA announced the largest competitive grant award in our history: $25 million through the U.S. Department of Transportation’s FY2026 BUILD Grant program.
 This investment is about so much more than autonomous vehicles. It’s about building the people, infrastructure, technology, and expertise Chattanooga needs to lead the future of transportation.
 Here at Shuttle Park South, CARTA and UTC will create a permanent Mobility & Innovation Command Center to oversee and support the next generation of transit technology.
 A new Live-Learning Lab will connect technology with education, giving students, researchers, and CARTA employees opportunities to learn and develop skills in autonomous systems, transportation technology, AI, data, cybersecurity, and more.
 Building on the City of Chattanooga and UTC’s SMART Grant work and EPB’s technology infrastructure, this project will help create a more connected and innovative transportation system.
 Most importantly, we’re not just bringing the future of transportation to Chattanooga and we’re preparing Chattanoogans to lead it.
 Over the next three years, CARTA and our partners will build the infrastructure, develop the workforce, test new technology, and create expertise that can serve our community for decades to come.

 The City of Red Bank has awarded $50,000 to 10 local nonprofit organizations through the final year of its three-year ARPA-funded grant program. These organizations support youth programs, food security, education, workforce development, environmental stewardship, animal welfare, and community recreation across Red Bank.
 This year’s grants will help fund programs at organizations including Red Bank Awards Final $50,000's listed recipients such as Be The Change Youth Initiative, La Paz Chattanooga, the Red Bank Community Food Pantry, WaterWays, White Oak Bicycle Co-op, and others serving local residents.
 Over the past three years, Red Bank has invested approximately $150,000 in nonprofit organizations that strengthen and support our community. Thank you to the nonprofits, volunteers, and community partners who continue to make a difference in the lives of Red Bank residents. ❤️

Christopher Taylor (DOB: 05/16/1970) contacted one of our undercover officers posing as a minor and solicited them for sexual activity. Investigators tracked Taylor to Kansas, where he was arrested. Taylor is currently being held in Franklin County, Kansas awaiting extradition on the following charges:
 - Rape of a child for soliticing a 12-year-old
 - Aggravated Statutory Rape for soliciting a 16-year-old
 - Especially Aggravated Sexual Exploitation of a Minor x2
 - Offense of Soliciting Sexual Exploition of a Minor by Electronic Means
 The charges and allegations referenced in this post are merely accusations of criminal conduct and not evidence. A defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt and convicted through due process of law..

items.content_text:
Bilateral official development assistance (ODA) for health is projected to fall to its lowest level in almost two decades.
 ODA is financial support from governments promoting the economic development and welfare of developing countries.
 #OECD projections show that bilateral ODA for health could decline by 29-46% between 2024 and 2026, equivalent to a reduction of USD 5-8 billion. This would bring support back to levels not seen since 2008.
 The decline follows the sharp increase in health ODA during the COVID-19 pandemic. By 2026, funding is projected to be 63% below its 2022 peak, with further reductions expected beyond 2026 as major providers continue to implement multi-year cuts.
 Health was the third-largest sector for bilateral ODA in 2024, receiving USD 17.6 billion, after humanitarian aid and support to government and civil society. The scale of the projected reductions could therefore have significant implications for countries that rely on external financing to support their health systems. 
 Explore the latest data on ODA for health ➡️ https://brnw.ch/21x5pb1

🚨 WARNING SHOTS FIRED 🚨
 Listen, I try to stay in my lane in the City of Chattanooga, which is in Hamilton County. But today I’m speaking as something else too:
 A County District 11 RESIDENT and VOTER.
 What happened today at the Hamilton County Commission was shameful.
 Our District 11 School Board representative resigned with TWO YEARS remaining in the term. There was a path available that would have allowed District 11 voters to choose who represents us in the November election.
 Instead, the Commission chose not to take that path.
 Yes, I heard the discussion about the law going back to 1925.
 But don’t let the semantics fool you.
 Current Tennessee law also provides a path for an appointed School Board member to serve until a successor is elected and qualified.
 And we have a general election THIS NOVEMBER.
 The path was simple:
 1️⃣ Declare the seat vacant.
 ⬇️
 2️⃣ Make the temporary appointment.
 ⬇️
 3️⃣ Let the parties caucus.
 ⬇️
 4️⃣ Let independents qualify.
 ⬇️
 5️⃣ Put the candidates on the November ballot.
 ⬇️
 🗳️ LET. THE. PEOPLE. VOTE.
 That’s it.
 Clean. Simple. Easy.
 Instead, District 11 voters will not get to choose our School Board representative at the ballot box this November.
 And THAT is my problem.
 The real question is simple:
 If there was a lawful path to let the people vote, why was letting the people vote such a problem?
 👏🏾 Kudos to MY District 11 Commissioner Montrell Besley for standing up for the people he represents and supporting our opportunity to choose our representative.
 🚨 Warning shots fired.
 Because when politics begins to have more power than people, every voter should pay attention.
 Today it’s District 11.
 Tomorrow it could be your district.
 Whether you’re a Democrat, Republican, Independent, or none of the above, this should not be complicated:
 🗳️ OUR DISTRICT. OUR REPRESENTATIVE. WHY NOT OUR VOTE?
 ⚠️ POLITICS OVER PEOPLE IS NEVER OKAY.
 And as we navigate moments like this, I’m reminded of what Scripture requires of us:
 🙏🏾 “Act justly. Love mercy. Walk humbly with your God.” — Micah 6:8

items.title: We are deeply saddened by the passing of Shane Morrow, a dedicated community leader and visionary. Shane gave so much of...
items.content_text:
We are deeply saddened by the passing of Shane Morrow, a dedicated community leader and visionary.
 Shane gave so much of his time, energy and heart to making Chattanooga a better place. Through his leadership and commitment to others, he touched countless lives and helped make our community stronger.
Shane Reynald Morrow, beloved life partner, musician, artist, community builder, helper, connector, and visionary, passed away August 26, 2026 at the age of 57.
 Born in Bridgeport, Connecticut, Shane was the son of the late Cheryl Morrow Tinsley and Larry Black. He graduated from Central High School in Bridgeport and continued his education at Housatonic Community College, where he completed a two-year program in computer programming.
 Shane was a musician at heart. Coming from generations of piano players, music was both a gift and a language through which he connected with others. But Shane's passion extended far beyond his own creativity. He believed deeply in the power of the arts to bring people together, preserve culture, create opportunity, and make communities stronger.
 Shane was, above all, a helper and a connector.
 He had a remarkable ability to see possibility in people, sometimes before they could see it in themselves. He connected artists to opportunities, people to resources, friends to one another, and ideas to the people who could help make them real. If someone needed help, Shane looked for a way to provide it. If someone had a gift that deserved to be seen, he looked for a stage. If there was a door that needed to be opened, Shane would open it.
 That spirit was at the heart of Jazzanooga, which Shane co-founded with his life partner, James McKissic. What began in 2011 as a celebration of Jazz Appreciation Month grew into an organization dedicated to celebrating Chattanooga's rich Black musical heritage, expanding access to the arts, and creating opportunities for artists and communities too often overlooked.
 Shane believed that the arts should belong to everyone. He worked to remove the financial, cultural, and social barriers that could prevent people from experiencing them. Under his leadership, Jazzanooga grew from a festival into a year-round community arts organization, eventually evolving into RISE Chattanooga, Responsive Initiatives for Social Empowerment.
 Through RISE, Shane's vision grew even broader. Music remained central, but so did entrepreneurship, cultural preservation, professional development for creatives, community empowerment, and creating opportunities for Black and Brown artists, businesses, and neighborhoods. Whether through a concert in a city park, a program for young musicians, support for a creative entrepreneur, or simply introducing two people who needed to know one another, Shane understood that building community was about building relationships.
 Shane's impact cannot be measured only by the organizations he founded, the programs he created, or the performances he helped bring to Chattanooga. His true legacy lives in people: the artists he encouraged, the young people he inspired, the entrepreneurs he supported, the friendships he nurtured, the introductions he made, the opportunities he created, and the many people he helped simply because helping was part of who he was.
 Shane was preceded in death by his parents, Cheryl Morrow Tinsley and Larry Black.
 He leaves behind his partner of nearly thirty years, James McKissic, his baby, Zora McKissic; his aunts and uncles Russel Ray, David Ray, Barney Ray, Mary Ray, Lance Morrow, Brent Morrow, Jason Morrow, Eugenia McCallister; and an extended network of cousins, friends, artists, musicians, colleagues, neighbors, and community members whose lives were enriched by Shane’s friendship, generosity, creativity, and care. 
 Shane believed that creativity could transcend barriers and that everyone deserved the opportunity to experience the joy, dignity, and connection that the arts can provide. He spent his life putting that belief into practice.
 The music, relationships, organizations, and community Shane helped build will continue. And in each person he connected to another, each artist he encouraged to step onto a stage, each idea he helped become reality, and each person he stopped to help along the way, a part of Shane remains.
 His was a life of creativity, service, connection, and love. And the community he spent so much of his life building will carry his spirit forward. 
 The community is invited to join family and friends of Shane Morrow in a celebration of his life through music and the arts on September 20, 2026, 4:00 pm at the Walker Theater in the Soldiers and Sailors Memorial Auditorium, 399 McCallie Avenue Chattanooga, TN 37402. In lieu of flowers, the family invites you to honor Shane’s memory with a donation to the Sankofa Fund for Civic Engagement. Donations will support youth music programs in Chattanooga, reflecting Shane’s love of music, the arts, and the importance of creating opportunities for young people in our community.
 To make a donation, please visit:
 https://cfgc.fcsuite.com/erp/donate
 Select “Sankofa Fund”, and follow the prompts to complete your gift.
 Your generosity is a meaningful way to celebrate Shane’s life and help carry forward his legacy through music and the arts

Something BIG is coming to Rossville, GA!
 Since 2016, Preserve Chattanooga has partnered with UTC’s Interior Architecture and Design Program to give students real-world experience in historic preservation and adaptive reuse.
 For this year’s senior thesis project, students are taking on the historic Peerless Mill in Rossville, Georgia. Over the next two semesters, they’ll reimagine what this remarkable 32-acre site could become, developing innovative design solutions that give the mill new life while honoring its historic character.
 Today, Tyler Cauble led the students on their initial site visit, helping them begin to understand the property, its history, and its incredible potential. Their work will culminate in a final exhibition at the end of the academic year, and we can’t wait to see their visions take shape.
 To learn more about Peerless Mill, visit tylercauble.com/peerless-mill.
 #HistoricPreservation #AdaptiveReuse #PeerlessMill #UTC #ThisIsHistoric

items.content_text:
River City Company is delighted to announce that our Emerging Producers program has received the 2026 International Downtown Association Pinnacle Award for Economic Development! Today, Tess Rollins, Director of Programs & Events, accepted the award on behalf of River City Company. 
 The IDA Pinnacle Awards are among the highest honors in urban place management, recognizing creative and innovative work happening in downtowns around the world. We’re incredibly grateful for this recognition, but even more proud of the people who have made Emerging Producers what it is today, including every producer who has been part of the program since it began in 2024. 
 Emerging Producers was created to help cultivate the next generation of event producers in Downtown Chattanooga. Through education, mentorship, and hands-on experience, the program gives aspiring producers the tools and support to bring their own public events to life. As we near the end of our third year, we continue to see that impact across Chattanooga as Emerging Producers graduates create events that bring new ideas, experiences, and perspectives to our city. 
 Thank you to the River City Company team, our Emerging Producers committee and mentors for the time and guidance they’ve given to this program, and to the Lyndhurst Foundation for believing in this work and helping make it possible. This award belongs to everyone who has been part of Emerging Producers along the way. 
 https://downtown.org/innovative-projects/emerging-producers/

Tennessee American Water Provides Additional PFAS Settlement Credit to Customers
  
 Latest credit of nearly $12 brings total PFAS settlement proceeds to more than $71 per customer
  
  
 CHATTANOOGA, TN (August 31, 2026) – Tennessee American Water announced that they are applying additional credits to customers’ bills as a result of the company's receipt of proceeds from settlements reached with manufacturers of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS). 
  
 Today, Tennessee American Water issued an $11.92 bill credit to all active water customer accounts as of August 28, 2026. The credit distributes recent settlement proceeds the company received from PFAS manufacturers to customers. 
  
 The Tennessee Public Utility Commission approved a plan that enables Tennessee American Water to provide PFAS settlement funds directly to customers through bill credits as the funds are received. Including this latest credit, customers have received a total of over $71 per account from PFAS-related settlements to date.  Tennessee American Water issued a credit of $59.36 to customers in March of this year to all active accounts at that time.  
  
 The company is committed to complying with all drinking water standards and is taking appropriate actions to meet new PFAS regulations as they are implemented. Tennessee American Water is investing over $45 million in capital improvements across their service territories to continue providing safe, clean, reliable and affordable water service. For more information about PFAS and the steps Tennessee American Water is taking to address them, visit the company's PFAS information page. 
  
 About American Water  
 American Water (NYSE: AWK) is the largest regulated water and wastewater utility company in the United States. With a history dating back to 1886 and celebrating 140 years in 2026, We Keep Life Flowing® by providing safe, clean, reliable and affordable drinking water and wastewater services to approximately 14 million people with regulated operations in 14 states and on 19 military installations. American Water’s approximately 7,000 talented professionals leverage their significant expertise and the company’s national size and scale to achieve excellent outcomes for the benefit of customers, employees, investors and other stakeholders. For more information, visit amwater.com and join American Water on LinkedIn, Facebook, X and Instagram.   
  
 About Tennessee American Water 
 Tennessee American Water, a subsidiary of American Water, is the largest regulated water utility in the state with approximately 100 dedicated employees working to provide safe, clean, reliable and affordable water services to approximately 425,000 people in Tennessee and north Georgia. 
  
 For more information, visit www.tennesseeamwater.com and connect with us on Facebook, X, Instagram, LinkedIn and YouTube.

 As funding declines, support for pandemic preparedness, prevention and response (PPR) is also at risk, raising concerns about recipient countries' ability to respond to future health crises. 
 ➡️ Almost 80% of PPR financing in low-income countries comes from external sources, including ODA. 
 ➡️ Spending on pandemic PPR is more than 30 times lower per capita in low-income countries than in advanced economies. 
 ➡️ Countries already responding to disease outbreaks are also projected to face substantial reductions in health ODA.  
 Between 2024 and 2026, bilateral health ODA could fall by 53.5% in Uganda and 46.6% in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where Ebola outbreaks are ongoing. 
 Pandemic preparedness is a global public good. 
 As outbreaks of infectious diseases become more frequent and widespread, reduced investment in preparedness and response could increase health risks well beyond the countries directly affected.

items.content_text:
Africa is already experiencing the impacts of climate change, yet key data on climate policies remain limited or unavailable across the continent. 
 This makes it harder for governments to design effective climate policies and target action where it is needed most. 
 A new report by the #OECD, GGGI, the World Bank and OECD's Sahel and West Africa Club helps close these information gaps. It brings together data on climate risks and climate policies across 28 African countries, using the #OECD Climate Actions and Policies Measurement Framework. 
 The report shows that:
 ➡️Climate policy action in Africa has more than doubled between 2010 and 2024, but have slowed down significantly from 2021 onwards.  
 ➡️Africa already experiences the most severe droughts across all continents, indicating risks to agriculture. 
 ➡️A very high-emissions scenario could lead to a doubling of hot days across the continent by 2100.
 Explore the report: https://brnw.ch/21x5lRG

Message From Your Sheriff - Flock/ Motorola LPR Cameras Paused
 As of today, I have directed staff within your Hamilton County Sheriff’s Office to begin the process of pausing the Flock License Plate Recognition (LPR) and Motorola LPR programs managed by our Office. 
 This directive, being weighed over several weeks, encompasses multiple factors that have contributed to this decision. 
 The primary factor is the tremendous concern regarding public data and potential misuse of what is captured. 
 Within the HCSO program, your Sheriff’s Office oversees approximately 70 cameras across Hamilton County.
 As your elected Sheriff, I truly believe in LPR technology and its ability to combat criminal activity in Hamilton County and those criminals who are here to cause harm and turmoil.
 At my direction, HCSO Command Staff will continue to work through factors of concern that led me to this decision to pause until I am confident that all areas of these concerns are addressed. 
 During this time, I call on our state and federal leaders to begin a conversation into what is best for our state, our country, and the protection of the citizens of Hamilton County.

items.content_text:
HCSO Recovers Homemade Explosives, Weapons, Stolen Property
 Hamilton County, TN – On August 28, 2026, the HCSO Criminal Investigations Unit conducted a controlled buy on Facebook Marketplace with a suspect who posted stolen items two days prior. A joint operation was then launched involving the HCSO Criminal Investigations Unit, Narcotics and Special Operations Unit, alongside Uniformed Services deputies.
 HCSO detectives and patrol deputies initiated a traffic stop on Hixson Pike, where the suspect was found in possession of the stolen property. Deputies executed a search warrant at the suspect’s home and three storage units, where deputies located drugs, drug paraphernalia, a loaded 9mm handgun, an altered shotgun, an altered flare gun, a large quantity of ammunition, two explosive military hand grenade simulators, 15 homemade explosives, and approximately $40,000--$60,000 in stolen property.
 The stolen property has been linked to multiple thefts and burglaries being investigated by the Hamilton County Sheriff's Office and the Chattanooga Police Department.
 The suspect, James Robert Bowman, was taken into custody and faces the following charges:
 • Prohibited Weapons x17
 • Felon in Possession of a Firearm x3
 • Burglary
 • Theft of Property
 The HCSO would like to thank the Chattanooga Police Department Bomb Squad and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) for their assistance in this investigation.
 Additional charges are pending in relation to the investigation. This information is preliminary and subject to change. No further details are available.

There’s more than 130 years of history behind the doors of one of UTC’s most distinctive buildings. 🏛️
 Built in 1896, the Isbester House at 551 Oak St. was once the home of Chattanooga industrialist Caleb B. Isbester. Over the years, the historic Queen Anne Revival home served as a mayor’s residence, a men’s dormitory and professional offices before returning to UTC in 2011.
 Following extensive restoration and preservation, the building became known as Alumni House in 2016. Today, it serves as an administrative headquarters for campus, housing the offices of the chancellor, provost and director of economic and workforce development.
 🔗  Discover the story behind one of UTC’s historic landmarks and the people who helped shape Chattanooga: https://blog.utc.edu/…/if-these-walls-could-talk-alumni-ho…/

Get ready to enjoy your lunch hour with a side of free music — River City Company's annual Noontunes concert series will return this Thursday in Miller Park. 🎶
 From 12-1 p.m., you can hear tunes from our local music scene, grab a bite from a food truck, and enjoy lawn games every Thursday during the month of September. Come take a break with us, Chattanooga!

items.title: Congressman Chuck Fleischmann has successfully secured $3 million in federal funding to advance the UTC Translational Re...
items.content_text:
Congressman Chuck Fleischmann has successfully secured $3 million in federal funding to advance the UTC Translational Research Program. This significant investment underscores UTC’s commitment to pioneering research and innovation that directly benefits the community and the region.
 The funding, awarded as part of a federal appropriations package, will support UTC’s efforts to bridge the gap between scientific discovery and real-world application. The Translational Research Program at UTC focuses on translating groundbreaking research into practical solutions.
 🔗  Read more here: https://blog.utc.edu/…/congressman-chuck-fleischmann-secur…/
